title: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
gist: An interactive MIT Technology Review piece uses puzzles that have stumped frontier LLMs to map where machine cognition still lags humans: spatial/mental rotation, subtly altered classics that trigger memorized answers, image-form ARC-AGI grids, and combinatorial problems past roughly six elements. Progress is rapid (NYT Connections solve rates went from 18% in late 2024 to near-perfect by early 2025), but the failure modes reveal that model 'reasoning' often rests on memorization and byzantine, non-generalizable rules rather than the simple visual concepts humans use.

insights.claim: Frontier AI puzzle-solving capability is improving extremely fast: a Columbia University team found in late 2024 that the best models solved only 18% of NYT Connections puzzles, yet by early 2025 some models solved them near-perfectly every time.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Benchmark saturation within months is the norm; discount any 'AI can't do X' claim with a short shelf life when underwriting AI capability trajectories.
insights.quote: even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some models could solve them near perfectly every time
insights.locator: Judged purely on its puzzling skills

insights.claim: Puzzles and games have been the core evaluation instrument for AI since the field's origin — the term 'machine learning' was popularized in a 1959 article by IBM's Arthur Samuel about a checkers-playing algorithm, with chess and Go serving as later test beds.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Game/puzzle benchmarks remain the industry's canonical proof-of-progress marketing; expect capability claims to keep being framed this way.
insights.locator: Puzzles and games have been central

insights.claim: Where models succeed and fail on puzzles — and where humans still beat them — is a diagnostic window into AI's real strengths and weaknesses, more informative than aggregate benchmark scores.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Failure-mode analysis (not leaderboard rank) is the better due-diligence lens for judging whether a model is fit for a given commercial task.

themes.theme: Spatial reasoning is a persistent weak spot

insights.claim: Despite having visual-input capabilities, today's language models still fail abysmally at mental rotation problems, unable to manipulate 3D objects the way architects and mechanical engineers do — the talk of 'world models' notwithstanding.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: AI substitution risk in spatially intensive professions (architecture, mechanical engineering, robotics planning) is overstated near-term; world-model hype should be tested against mental-rotation-style evals.
insights.quote: For all the talk of how world models can help AI understand physical environments, LLMs still don’t seem to be able to manipulate 3D objects the way spatial thinkers like architects and mechanical engineers can.

insights.claim: A 2024 study by Google and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers showed that when Knights-and-Knaves logic puzzles are slightly varied from training-set versions, models whiz past the key differences and answer with what they memorized.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Training-data contamination inflates benchmark scores; enterprise buyers should test models on perturbed versions of their tasks before trusting reported evals.
insights.quote: the model may whiz by key differences and respond with what it memorized

insights.claim: On SimpleBench, questions deliberately resemble more complicated problems models likely saw in training; unspecialized humans spot the trick while even top-tier frontier models trip.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Adversarial, contamination-resistant benchmarks like SimpleBench are the cleaner signal of genuine reasoning ability across model releases.

insights.claim: An LLM's vast trained-in memory is simultaneously an asset (trivia-level recall beyond humans) and a liability (pattern-matching to memorized answers instead of reading the actual problem).
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for AI product risk: the same scale that drives capability drives brittle memorization errors in novel-but-familiar-looking cases (e.g., legal, medical edge cases).
insights.quote: That’s an asset for outcompeting humans at trivia, but it can also be a liability.

insights.claim: Models perform better on ARC-AGI puzzles when each grid is fed as a string of numbers encoding cell colors rather than as an image — visual perception, not abstraction alone, is a binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Input representation materially changes measured capability; multimodal 'vision' features may lag text pipelines more than marketing suggests.
insights.quote: Models do better on ARC puzzles when they receive each grid not as an image but as a string of numbers that encodes the color of each cell.

insights.claim: Research suggests that even when models answer ARC-AGI questions correctly, they often rely on byzantine, non-generalizable rules, whereas humans draw on simple visual concepts — right answers are not evidence of human-like generalization.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Correct outputs can hide fragile mechanisms; robustness under distribution shift, not accuracy, is the metric to watch for AGI claims tied to ARC scores.
insights.quote: they often do so using byzantine and non-­generalizable rules, whereas humans draw on simple visual concepts

insights.claim: Models have improved substantially on ARC-AGI over the past year, yet specific puzzles still stump them entirely.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: ARC-AGI remains one of the few unsaturated benchmarks; movement on it is a leading indicator worth tracking for genuine reasoning progress.

insights.claim: On intuition-trap problem suites that invert SimpleBench, humans give knee-jerk wrong answers while models respond deliberatively and get them right — AI does not share many human cognitive biases.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: There is a real commercial niche for AI as a bias-checking layer on human judgment (underwriting, diligence, forecasting), separate from the automation narrative.
insights.quote: humans often give knee-jerk answers, whereas models will respond deliberatively

insights.claim: An Apple study found LLMs ace simple Tower of Hanoi and river-crossing puzzles but begin to falter once the number of disks or people reaches six or more — capability collapses as combinatorial complexity scales.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Multi-step agentic workflows may hit similar depth limits; stress-test agent products on long-horizon combinatorial tasks before assuming reliability.
insights.quote: As the number of disks or people hits six and higher, the models began to falter.

insights.claim: Researchers at the University of Washington, Stanford, and the Allen Institute for AI (ZebraLogic) found LLMs struggle analogously with logic grid puzzles requiring multi-clue deduction, corroborating the complexity-scaling limit beyond Apple's result.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: The scaling-limit finding replicates across independent labs and puzzle types — treat it as a structural property of current LLMs, not a one-off headline.

insights.claim: The viral Apple reasoning paper is contested: commentators question whether its results reveal a unique limitation of LLM reasoning or merely that error rates naturally rise as complexity piles up — the same pattern humans show.
insights.speaker: Grace Huckins
insights.so_what: Do not over-trade 'LLMs can't reason' headlines; the interpretive debate is unresolved and the bearish reading of the Apple paper is not consensus among researchers.
insights.quote: commentators questioned whether the results reveal a unique limitation of LLM reasoning—or just that it’s normal to make errors as complexity piles up
